author: A Robot
objectives: Students will determine the steric number of a central atom from its Lewis structure by counting bonding pairs and lone pairs.
Students will predict the electron-domain geometry of a molecule from its steric number, identifying the linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, or octahedral arrangement.
Students will distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry, and identify the molecular shape produced when one or more domains is a lone pair.
Students will explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, and predict the direction of bond-angle deviations from idealized values.
Students will apply VSEPR predictions to specific molecules and compare predicted geometries to experimentally observed structures.

modules.description: This module introduces VSEPR theory and demonstrates the five fundamental electron-domain geometries.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Predict the electron-domain geometry of a molecule from its steric number.
Identify the linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, or octahedral arrangement.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduction to VSEPR Theory. The central atom is shown with two electron domains that will arrange themselves to minimize repulsion.
clips.narration: Welcome to the VSEPR theory lab. VSEPR stands for Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion. This theory helps us predict the 3D shape of molecules.

clips.changeMeaning: Two electron domains arrange linearly, demonstrating the minimized repulsion in a linear electron domain geometry.
clips.narration: When a central atom has two electron domains, they arrange themselves 180 degrees apart, forming a linear electron domain geometry. This minimizes repulsion.

clips.changeMeaning: Adding a third electron domain, demonstrating trigonal planar geometry.
clips.narration: With three electron domains, the geometry becomes trigonal planar. The domains spread out to approximately 120 degrees from each other.

clips.changeMeaning: Adding a fourth electron domain, demonstrating tetrahedral geometry.
clips.narration: Four electron domains around a central atom adopt a tetrahedral electron domain geometry. The domains are oriented towards the corners of a tetrahedron, with bond angles of approximately 109.5 degrees.

clips.changeMeaning: Demonstrating the complex arrangements for five and six electron domains, including trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral geometries.
clips.narration: For five and six electron domains, we see more complex arrangements: trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral, respectively. These arrangements also maximize the distance between electron domains.

modules.moduleName: Molecular Geometry: Lone Pairs and Molecular Shapes
modules.description: This module explores how lone pairs affect molecular geometry, leading to different molecular shapes.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry.
Identify the molecular shape produced when one or more domains is a lone pair.
Explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduction to molecular geometry and lone pairs. A central atom with two bonding domains and one lone pair is shown.
clips.narration: Now, let's consider how lone pairs affect molecular geometry. Lone pairs are regions of electron density that also repel bonding pairs.

clips.changeMeaning: Demonstrating bent molecular geometry. The lone pair pushes the bonding domains closer together.
clips.narration: With two bonding domains and one lone pair, the electron domains arrange in a trigonal planar fashion. However, the molecular geometry is bent. Notice how the lone pair, being more diffuse, pushes the bonding pairs closer together, resulting in a bond angle slightly less than 120 degrees.

clips.changeMeaning: Demonstrating trigonal pyramidal geometry. A central atom with three bonding domains and one lone pair.
clips.narration: When we have three bonding domains and one lone pair, like in ammonia, the electron domains still arrange tetrahedrally. But the molecular geometry is trigonal pyramidal. The lone pair occupies more space, compressing the bond angles from the ideal 109.5 degrees.

clips.changeMeaning: Demonstrating octahedral and square pyramidal geometries. A central atom with six electron domains (five bonding, one lone pair).
clips.narration: In cases with six electron domains, such as sulfur hexafluoride, we see octahedral electron domain geometry. If one of these domains is a lone pair, as in iodine pentafluoride, the molecular geometry becomes square pyramidal. The lone pair again exerts greater repulsion, causing distortions.

modules.description: This module applies VSEPR theory to predict and visualize the shapes of common molecules like methane, water, and ammonia.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Apply VSEPR predictions to specific molecules.
Compare predicted geometries to experimentally observed structures.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduction to real-world molecules. Methane molecule is displayed, illustrating perfect tetrahedral geometry.
clips.narration: VSEPR theory is incredibly powerful because it accurately predicts the shapes of real molecules. Let's look at some examples.

clips.changeMeaning: Methane molecule displayed, showing tetrahedral geometry.
clips.narration: Methane (CH4) has four electron domains around the central carbon atom, all of which are bonding pairs. This results in a perfect tetrahedral electron domain and molecular geometry, with bond angles of 109.5 degrees.

clips.changeMeaning: Water molecule is displayed, showing bent geometry with a smaller bond angle due to lone pair repulsion.
clips.narration: Now consider water (H2O). The central oxygen atom has two bonding pairs and two lone pairs, giving it four electron domains. The electron domain geometry is tetrahedral, but the molecular geometry is bent due to the two lone pairs, resulting in bond angles of approximately 104.5 degrees.

clips.changeMeaning: Ammonia molecule is displayed, showing trigonal pyramidal geometry with compressed bond angles.
clips.narration: Finally, let's look at ammonia (NH3). The central nitrogen atom has three bonding pairs and one lone pair. This gives four electron domains, leading to a tetrahedral electron domain geometry. However, the molecular geometry is trigonal pyramidal, with bond angles slightly compressed from the ideal tetrahedral value.

clips.changeMeaning: Summary of VSEPR predictions and their significance in understanding molecular properties and reactivity.
clips.narration: As you can see, VSEPR theory provides a robust framework for understanding and predicting the shapes of molecules, which is crucial for understanding their chemical properties and reactivity.
